rows.stem:
The correct name of the given reaction is
\(\mathrm{Ar-N_2^+\,X^-} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Cu\ powder}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{Ar-Br + N_2}\).
rows.solution:
The reaction is the GATTERMANN REACTION.

A diazonium salt is warmed with the halogen acid in the presence of COPPER POWDER, and the diazonium group is replaced by the halide while nitrogen escapes as a gas:
\(\mathrm{Ar{-}N_2^+X^-} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Cu\ powder}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{Ar{-}Br} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The distinction from SANDMEYER'S reaction is exactly the form of the copper. Sandmeyer uses a COPPER(I) SALT — copper(I) bromide in this case — while Gattermann uses copper POWDER together with the halogen acid, the metal generating the copper(I) species in situ. Both reach the same product; Gattermann's yields are generally lower.

Of the other options, Gabriel phthalimide synthesis makes primary aliphatic amines from alkyl halides, the carbylamine reaction detects primary amines, and Hofmann bromamide degradation shortens an amide by one carbon. None involves a diazonium salt.

rows.stem: Visha took 4 test-tubes namely A, B, C & D containing \(\mathrm{CH_3CH = CH_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH = CH_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH = CH - CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C = CH_2}\) respectively and tried to convert them into tertbutylalcohol. She carried out acid catalysed hydration reaction on every alkene. Out of the four test-tubes, the one which will give desired result is
rows.solution:
The desired result comes from test-tube D, which holds 2-METHYLPROPENE, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2}\).

Acid-catalysed hydration follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE: the proton adds to the doubly bonded carbon that already carries more hydrogens, so the hydroxyl goes to the OTHER one — the more substituted carbon.

In 2-methylpropene the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) end takes the proton and the hydroxyl goes to the carbon already bearing two methyl groups, which then carries three carbons and an \(-\mathrm{OH}\):
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^+}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH}\)

That is tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

A TERTIARY alcohol needs the hydroxyl to land on a carbon already carrying three carbons, and only a BRANCHED alkene can supply one. The three straight-chain alkenes in tubes A, B and C would all give secondary alcohols.

rows.stem: Van’t Hoff factor for \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution assuming the complete dissociation is
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor for potassium chloride is 2.

The factor is the ratio of the number of particles ACTUALLY present in solution to the number expected from the formula. Potassium chloride dissociates completely:
\(\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}\)
giving TWO ions from each formula unit, so \(i = 2\).

The consequence is measurable: a one molal solution of potassium chloride depresses the freezing point of water by \(2 \times 1{\cdot}86 = 3{\cdot}72\) K, twice what a one molal solution of glucose would give.

A factor of 1 would mean no dissociation at all, as with glucose or urea; a factor below 1 would mean ASSOCIATION, as with acetic acid dimerising in benzene.

rows.stem: Dilution affects both molar conductivity as well as conductivity. Effect of dilution on both is

options.label: A
options.text: molar conductivity decreases whereas conductivity increases on dilution.

options.label: B
options.text: molar conductivity increases whereas conductivity decreases on dilution.

rows.solution:
MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY INCREASES whereas CONDUCTIVITY DECREASES on dilution.

The two behave oppositely because they are referred to different things.

CONDUCTIVITY is the conductance of a fixed VOLUME of solution — the amount held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. Diluting puts fewer ions in that volume, so fewer charge carriers sit between the electrodes and the conductivity falls.

MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY refers the conductance to a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte, one mole, however much solvent that mole is spread through:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}\)
Dilution lets the ions move further apart, so they drag on one another less, and for a weak electrolyte it lets more of it dissociate. Both effects raise the value, which climbs towards the limiting \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\).

rows.stem: Which of the following cell is used in inverter ?
rows.solution:
The LEAD STORAGE CELL is used in an inverter.

An inverter must store a large amount of energy and be RECHARGEABLE, and the lead storage battery is the standard secondary cell for the purpose: applying an external voltage greater than its own reverses both electrode reactions and restores lead and lead dioxide from the lead sulphate that coats them on discharge.

It is built from a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide as the cathode, in about 38% sulphuric acid, and it delivers a large current — which is also why it starts cars.

The dry cell and the mercury cell are PRIMARY cells and cannot be recharged; a fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel from outside and does not store energy at all.

rows.stem: In which of the following molecules, C atom marked with asterisk is chiral ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the four candidate molecules (I), (II), (III), (IV) are printed as DRAWN wedge-and-dash 3-D structures around a starred carbon, and the four options are only lists of those Roman numerals, so the stem names nothing at all without them. The drawings are deliberately NOT described here: naming the four substituents on each starred carbon is exactly the discrimination the question tests, so a text rendering would state the answer. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The chiral ones are II, III AND IV.

A carbon is CHIRAL when it carries FOUR DIFFERENT groups — that is what makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image. Check each starred carbon.

I carries \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\) and \(\mathrm{H}\) — TWO methyls, identical, so NOT chiral.
II carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.
III carries \(\mathrm{D}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.
IV carries \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2}\), \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{D}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.

Structures III and IV are worth pausing on: DEUTERIUM and HYDROGEN are different ISOTOPES of the same element, and that is enough to count as different groups. Structure I fails not on any isotope but on the repeated methyl.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{A + 2B \rightarrow C + D}\). The order of the reaction is

options.label: C
options.text: can’t be predicted as order is determined experimentally.

rows.solution:
The order CANNOT BE PREDICTED from the equation, because order is determined EXPERIMENTALLY.

This is the central lesson of chemical kinetics. The balanced equation \(\mathrm{A} + 2\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}\) is a statement of STOICHIOMETRY — how much of each substance is consumed and produced — and it says nothing about the MECHANISM.

Order depends on the mechanism, in particular on the slowest step. A reactant that appears in the balanced equation may not appear in the rate law at all if it enters only in a fast step, and a species that is not in the equation at all may appear in the rate law if it is a catalyst.

The three numerical options each assume the exponents can be read off the coefficients. That is true ONLY for an ELEMENTARY reaction — one occurring in a single step — and nothing here says this reaction is elementary.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Faraday’s second law of electrolysis
(b) Corrosion
rows.solution:
(a) FARADAY'S SECOND LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS states that when the SAME QUANTITY of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in SERIES, the amounts of the different substances liberated at the electrodes are proportional to their CHEMICAL EQUIVALENT WEIGHTS.

So passing one faraday through solutions of silver nitrate, copper sulphate and aluminium chloride in series deposits one equivalent of each — 108 g of silver, 31.75 g of copper and 9 g of aluminium — the differences following from the differing charges on the ions.

(b) CORROSION is the slow OXIDATION of a metal to undesirable products when it is exposed to air and moisture — a redox process in which the metal is oxidised by the surroundings.

The rusting of iron is the familiar case, where the product is hydrated iron(III) oxide, \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O}\). It is electrochemical in nature: one part of the metal surface acts as an anode, where iron is oxidised, and another as a cathode, where oxygen is reduced, with the moisture film serving as the electrolyte that joins them.

The tarnishing of silver and the green coating on copper are corrosion too.

rows.stem:
Classify the following sugars into monosaccharides and disaccharides :
Fructose, Lactose, Glucose, Maltose
rows.solution:
MONOSACCHARIDES: GLUCOSE and FRUCTOSE.
DISACCHARIDES: LACTOSE and MALTOSE.

A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit and cannot be hydrolysed to anything simpler; a disaccharide is two such units joined by a glycosidic linkage, so hydrolysis splits it into two.

Note the relationship within the list: maltose hydrolyses to two molecules of GLUCOSE, and lactose to glucose and galactose. Fructose is the ketose of the group, its carbonyl at \(\mathrm{C_2}\) rather than \(\mathrm{C_1}\).

All four are REDUCING sugars, each having an anomeric carbon free — fructose included, because in the alkaline test medium it isomerises to an aldose.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination compounds : (any three)
(a) \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl(ONO)]Cl}\)
(d) \(\mathrm{[Zn(OH)_4]^{2-}}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Three potassium ions give \(+3\) and six cyanido ligands \(-6\), so iron is \(+3\) and the complex is the ANION — which takes the -ate ending, built on the Latin stem for iron:
POTASSIUM HEXACYANIDOFERRATE(III)

(b) Two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) against an overall \(+2\), and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral, so platinum is \(+4\). The bracketed ligand takes bis- because its own name already contains a numerical prefix:
DICHLORIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)PLATINUM(IV) ION

(c) The chloride outside gives \(-1\); inside, four ammines are neutral while chlorido and nitrito each give \(-1\), so cobalt is \(+3\). The nitrite here is written \(-\mathrm{ONO}\), bound through OXYGEN, so it is named nitrito-O:
TETRAAMMINECHLORIDONITRITO-O-COBALT(III) CHLORIDE

(d) Four hydroxido ligands give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so zinc is \(+2\) and the complex is the anion:
TETRAHYDROXIDOZINCATE(II) ION

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(a) Haloalkanes react with NaCN to form both cyanides and isocyanides.
(b) Haloarenes do not undergo nucleophilic substitution reaction easily.
(c) Benzyl chloride gives \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the CYANIDE ION IS AMBIDENTATE — it has two different donor atoms and can attack through either.

Sodium cyanide is ionic, so it gives the free \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) ion in solution. That ion can donate its electron pair through the CARBON, giving the cyanide \(\mathrm{R{-}CN}\), or through the NITROGEN, giving the isocyanide \(\mathrm{R{-}NC}\).

Carbon is the better nucleophilic site, so the CYANIDE predominates — but the nitrogen route is open too, and some isocyanide accompanies it.

SILVER cyanide is the contrast: being largely COVALENT, it ties up the carbon's lone pair and leaves only the nitrogen free, so it gives the isocyanide as the MAIN product. One reagent gives a mixture, the other a clean switch.

(b) Because the carbon-halogen bond in a haloarene is far harder to break.

The halogen's lone pair is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond acquires partial DOUBLE BOND character: it is shorter and stronger, and a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute. The carbon carrying it is also \(sp^2\) rather than \(sp^3\), and an \(sp^2\) carbon holds the shared pair more tightly.

Two further obstacles: the ring's electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud REPELS an approaching nucleophile, and the PHENYL CATION that a unimolecular route would require is extremely unstable.

(c) Because the BENZYL CARBOCATION is stabilised by RESONANCE.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the carbocation forms, since that is the slow step. Benzyl chloride's chlorine sits on the \(sp^3\) carbon attached DIRECTLY to the ring, so when the chloride leaves the positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, spread over the ortho and para positions as well as the benzylic carbon.

An ordinary primary halide gives a plain primary cation with no such help, and reacts by this route far more slowly. Benzyl chloride is therefore unusual: a PRIMARY halide that nonetheless favours the unimolecular route.
